cells.tense: Here, with the pen, an ending that is due can be made without a scene.
cells.act: judge the hurt fairly after it has finished
cells.ask: Bring to mind something already over. In one sitting, decide plainly how much of it was fair to you, and set it down on paper. A single fair call.
cells.core:
You can end something without turning it into a performance. That's the strength here: when a thing in your actual life has run past its date, you can compost it and use the ground it leaves behind. The skill is real and it's already in your hands.

Where it lands well, an ending leaves the people closest to you less braced, and leaves you standing on ground you can plant in. The move now is to settle an old account — not by reopening who was right, but by judging it once, fairly, then setting it down. That frees the hours that go into turning it over, and turning it over is what keeps it open.
cells.sheetLine: You can close something without making a scene of it.
cells.verb: composting what's over into ground for what comes next

cells.tense: The ending hasn't arrived yet, and the space for it has been cleared already.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: Someone close to you is on the far side of an ending you've already walked through. Sit with what they feel about it, across one conversation, and leave it unfixed. Their pace isn't yours to set.
cells.core:
You are clearing ground for a change before it's due. Something is being ended in your head — a role, a way a group does its thing — and then you arrive and the furniture is already out. From where they stand, the chairs went out while they were still sitting in them.

The ability to end things isn't what's thin. What's thin is meeting a feeling that hasn't caught up with your pace. Let somebody stay inside their not-yet, without you having to agree with it. The turning that follows will be kinder, and it will carry the smell of the real thing instead of the plan.

cells.tense: The ending already happened, and one foot is still in the old doorway.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Ten minutes on something you want to begin, before it's clear. Then again tomorrow, and the day after. Keep the fire fed in small helpings.
cells.core:
Something finished and you kept the place set. The pot has yesterday's coffee in it, and you haven't sat down anywhere else. The starting part — the piece that used to carry you through an ending — isn't running. It isn't that the feeling is missing. You are at a doorway you already walked through, and the doorway is all you can see.

What's needed is a little life pointed at a direction that isn't about getting the old one back. A small move toward what draws you, before it's a plan. Feed the fire in small helpings; don't try to lay the whole path at once. The warmth you keep going does the rest, and it doesn't need the ending explained first.

cells.tense: The change is being led already by someone the account leaves out.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Do the stuck thing this hour — the call, the date, the move. Say nothing after it. One clean cut, and let it be one.
cells.core:
You are already making a way through, and you talk about it as though you were waiting for the path to show itself. Small decisions land; things move after you say something. What goes well shows in your hands — a stuck thing goes through because you took it, and the ground beneath the next move holds because you laid it.

What your account leaves out is that you made the turn. Sign one move: not a plan for the whole thing, one decision made on purpose, with your name on it. When a cut is owned, the hesitation around the rest gets shorter, and what's underfoot starts reading as your work.
